141.title: Holi (colors; Prahlada and the fire)
141.hook: the night before the colors: a boy who wouldn't stop saying the name, and the fire that couldn't burn him
141.howItsDone: On the full-moon night before Holi, many Hindu communities light a bonfire for Holika Dahan, retelling the story of Prahlada, walking around the fire, offering grain and coconut, and roasting new wheat or barley; the colors are played the next morning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Diwali ended: Lakshmi at the open door, a mountain lifted, a sister's blessing. Your line named all five days. Did you message someone who's like a sibling? Day one hundred and forty-one.

Everyone knows the pictures of Holi: people drenched in pink and green and yellow powder, laughing in the street. But that's the morning. The night before, in towns and villages and temple courtyards, people gather around a great pile of wood and dried branches, sometimes with a figure set on top. At the right moment, it's lit. The flames go up into the full-moon sky. People walk around it, throw in grain and coconuts, and hold up stalks of fresh wheat to roast. And somebody's grandmother tells the story, again, about a little boy who sat in a fire and walked out. Today: Holi, and the fire.
screen: `BEFORE THE COLORS, A BONFIRE.` → `THE FULL MOON, THE FLAMES.` → `A BOY WHO WALKED OUT OF THE FIRE.`

segments.voice: The story starts with a demon king, Hiranyakashipu. After years of fierce austerity, he wins an extraordinary protection: he can't be killed by man or beast, by day or by night, indoors or outdoors, on the ground or in the air, by any weapon. Believing himself unkillable, he orders everyone to worship him. Everyone does, except his own small son, Prahlada, who loves Vishnu and won't stop saying his name. The Bhagavata Purana tells how the father tries everything to break him, or to be rid of him: poison, trampling elephants, snakes, a fall from a cliff. Each time, the boy is kept safe, still saying the name. Then comes the part told at every Holi bonfire. The king's sister, Holika, has her own protection against fire. She takes Prahlada onto her lap and sits in a blazing pyre. And the fire goes the other way. Holika burns. Prahlada walks out untouched, still saying the name. Be honest about one thing: the Holika episode is told in later retellings and in the festival itself more than in the oldest versions of the story. But the heart is the same. Soon after, Vishnu comes as Narasimha, half man, half lion, at twilight, on the threshold, and ends the king's cruelty without breaking a single term of his protection. That's why the bonfire is called Holika Dahan, the burning of Holika. People circle it, the way you learned to walk around what's holy. Many throw in something from the harvest, and some carry a pinch of ash home. The fire takes what's cruel and leaves the faithful standing.
screen: `A KING WHO THOUGHT HE COULDN'T DIE.` · `A SON WHO WOULDN'T STOP SAYING THE NAME.` · `HOLIKA BURNS; PRAHLADA WALKS OUT.` · `HOLIKA DAHAN: THE BONFIRE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and picture the bonfire in front of you, the heat on your face, the full moon above. Now think of one thing you'd like to put on that fire. A grudge you're tired of carrying. A fear. A habit of cruelty, even toward yourself. Name it quietly. Then picture yourself tossing it in, and watching it catch and burn down to ash. If you pray, you can hold a name you honor the way Prahlada held his. If not, hold one steady breath after another. Stay by the fire. The bell holds the time.
Holi. The spring festival that begins the night before, with a bonfire for Prahlada, the boy the fire couldn't burn. Today's word.
Your line: Holi, colors, Prahlada and the fire. Today, write down the one thing you put on the fire, then tear up the paper and throw it away. Tomorrow, the colors. Day one hundred and forty-one.

142.title: Holi (colors; Prahlada and the fire)
142.hook: the morning after the fire: Krishna, Radha, a handful of color, and how to play it well
142.howItsDone: On Holi morning many Hindus greet elders first with a touch of gulal and a bow, then play with colored powder and water with family, friends and neighbors, sharing sweets like gujiya; in Braj the celebrations run for days.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Holi, and the night before it: the bonfire, and Prahlada walking out of the flames still saying the name. What did you put on the fire? Today, the morning after, and the colors. Day one hundred forty-two.

The fire has burned down to ash. Some people carry a little of it home, still warm, and touch it to their foreheads. Then everyone goes to bed, and the next morning the street belongs to color. Pink, green, yellow, a purple that won't wash out until Thursday. But why color? A bonfire makes sense for a story about fire. Nothing in Prahlada's story is pink. For the colors, people tell a different story, a smaller one, set in a village by a river, about a boy who was worried about his skin. And that story tells you how to play Holi well.
screen: `THE ASH, CARRIED HOME.` → `WHY COLOR?` → `A SECOND, SMALLER STORY.`

segments.voice: The boy is Krishna, growing up among cowherds in Braj, the country around Mathura and Vrindavan. He's dark. The old poems call his skin the color of a rain cloud. And the story people tell is that he goes to his foster mother, Yashoda, upset: why is Radha so fair, and I'm so dark? Yashoda laughs and tells him, go and put some color on her face, then. So he does. And Radha and her friends put color right back on him. That's the game. Be honest about this one: it's a story families and songs tell, not a scene from an old scripture. But in Braj it's everything. The towns where Krishna and Radha grew up keep Holi for days. In Barsana, Radha's village, women playfully chase the men from Krishna's village with long sticks, and the men hide behind shields and laugh. In Vrindavan, temples throw flower petals instead of powder. So how do people actually play? The color is called gulal, a soft powder. The old colors came from flowers, like the orange of the palash tree, soaked overnight; many families have gone back to gentle, natural colors. You start with elders: a pinch of color on their feet or cheeks, and a bow. You say happy Holi before you throw. You don't color someone who's said no, and you don't color a stranger who's clearly just trying to get to work. Then there's food: gujiya, little fried pastries full of sweet milk and nuts, and cool thandai to drink. The color is meant to be a greeting. Krishna didn't throw it to win. He threw it to close a distance, and he laughed when it came back.
screen: `A DARK BOY WORRIED ABOUT HIS SKIN.` · `GO AND COLOR HER FACE, THEN.` · `BRAJ KEEPS HOLI FOR DAYS.` · `ELDERS FIRST. ASK. THEN THROW.` · then, large: `COLOR CLOSES A DISTANCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: color someone, in your mind. Settle, and breathe out slowly. Think of a person you feel a little distance from. Not an enemy. Someone you drifted from, or someone you've been a bit cold with. Picture yourself walking up to them on Holi morning. You say happy Holi first. You wait for them to smile. Then a small pinch of pink on their cheek. And picture them putting color right back on you, and both of you laughing, looking a little ridiculous. Stay there, the two of you, the same messy color. The bell holds the time.
Holi. The spring festival: the fire the night before, for Prahlada, and the colors in the morning, for Krishna and Radha.
Your line: Holi, colors, Prahlada and the fire. Today, close one small distance. Write to them first, or greet the person you usually pass, and let them answer back. Day one hundred forty-two.

143.title: Navaratri (nine nights, nine forms; Durga)
143.hook: the gods pour their light into one form, and she rides out to meet the buffalo demon; then nine nights, nine faces
143.howItsDone: During Navaratri many Hindus honor the Goddess in nine forms, the Navadurga, one each night, with fasting, prayers and readings of the Devi Mahatmya; the tenth day, Vijayadashami or Dussehra, celebrates victory.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Holi in the morning: Krishna, Radha, and a pinch of color to close a distance. Did the color come back to you? Today, nine nights in a row. Day one hundred forty-three.

There's a demon with the head of a buffalo, and he can't be beaten. His name is Mahishasura. He has a boon that no man and no god can kill him, and he's used it to throw the gods out of heaven. They come together, furious and helpless. And the story says their anger turns into light. Out of Vishnu, out of Shiva, out of Brahma, out of every god, a blaze pours out, and all of it gathers into one form. She has many arms. Each god hands her a weapon. She rides a lion. And she laughs. Her name is Durga, and today we meet her nine faces.
screen: `A DEMON NO GOD CAN KILL.` → `THE GODS' LIGHT BECOMES ONE FORM.` → `SHE RIDES A LION.`

segments.voice: The story is told in the Devi Mahatmya, the Glory of the Goddess, a Sanskrit text of seven hundred verses that sits inside the Markandeya Purana. Durga fights the buffalo demon, and he keeps changing shape: a buffalo, a lion, a man with a sword, an elephant, the buffalo again. She meets every shape. In the end she pins him down and he's defeated. Many families say that battle took nine nights, and on the tenth day she won. That's where the festival gets its name. Nava, nine. Ratri, night. Navaratri. And here's the part that makes it a practice. Across the nine nights, many Hindus honor the Goddess in nine forms, one a night, called the Navadurga. She begins as Shailaputri, the daughter of the mountain. Then Brahmacharini, the young woman doing hard discipline. Then Chandraghanta, with a half-moon like a bell on her forehead. Kushmanda, who smiled the universe into being. Skandamata, mother of the war god Skanda. Katyayani, the warrior. Kalaratri, the dark night, fierce and frightening. Mahagauri, shining and calm. And Siddhidatri, the one who gives perfection. Nine faces: a daughter, a student, a warrior, a mother, the darkness itself, and then peace. Traditions differ on the details and the order, and some regions honor other forms. But the idea holds: the same power shows up differently on different nights. Some nights it's gentle. Some nights it's fierce. Both are her. And there's a surprise for those who wait: Navaratri comes twice a year, in spring and in autumn. The autumn one is the big one most people know.
screen: `THE DEMON KEEPS CHANGING SHAPE.` · `NAVA, NINE. RATRI, NIGHT.` · `NINE FORMS, ONE EACH NIGHT.` · `GENTLE OR FIERCE, BOTH ARE HER.` · then, large: `THE SAME POWER, NINE FACES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find your face for tonight. Settle, and breathe. Durga shows up as whatever the night needs. So ask: what does today need from me? Maybe the daughter of the mountain: steady, rooted. Maybe the student: disciplined, one more page. Maybe the warrior: say the hard thing. Maybe the mother: gentle with someone small. Maybe just the calm one. Don't overthink it. Let one face come. Then breathe as that face for a while, and notice how it sits in your shoulders. The bell holds the time.
Navaratri. Nine nights. The Goddess in nine forms, one a night, and on the tenth day she wins.
Your line: Navaratri, nine nights, nine forms, Durga. Today, pick the face the day needs, gentle or fierce, and wear it on purpose. Day one hundred forty-three.

144.title: Navaratri (nine nights, nine forms; Durga)
144.hook: a pot of earth with seeds, circles of dancers, dolls on steps, a goddess carried to the river: one festival, kept four ways
144.howItsDone: Many Hindus open Navaratri by setting up a pot as the Goddess's seat and sowing barley beside it, fast on some or all of the nine days, honor young girls as the Goddess in kanya puja on the eighth or ninth day, and keep the nights with garba in Gujarat, Durga Puja in Bengal and golu dolls in the South, ending on Vijayadashami.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Navaratri: the gods' light gathered into Durga, and nine forms, one a night. Which face did the day need from you? Today, how people actually keep those nine nights. Day one hundred forty-four.

It's the first morning of Navaratri in an apartment in Delhi. Before breakfast, someone spreads a layer of soil in a shallow tray and scatters barley over it. In the middle goes a clay pot of water, mango leaves tucked around its neck, a coconut on top. A lamp is lit beside it. Then everyone leaves for work and school. There's nothing to see yet. A pot and some dirt. But by the ninth day, that tray will be a small field of green. Yesterday was the story and the nine faces. Today is how the nights are actually kept, and it starts with that pot.
screen: `FIRST MORNING: SOIL AND SEEDS.` → `A POT, MANGO LEAVES, A COCONUT.` → `BY THE NINTH DAY: GREEN.`

segments.voice: It's called ghatasthapana. Ghata, the pot. Sthapana, setting it up. Many families invite the Goddess to be present in that pot for the nine days, and the barley beside it, jau in Hindi, is watched as it sprouts. Nobody hurries it. You water it, you keep the nights, and it comes up on its own. Then there's the fast, and people mean very different things by it. Some eat nothing until evening. Many simply set grain aside for nine days and cook with what's allowed instead: buckwheat flour, water chestnut flour, potatoes, fruit, milk. Some keep only the first and last days. The point isn't hunger. It's that every meal for nine days reminds you what time it is. Outside the house, you've met the big public shapes before: garba circles around a lamp in Gujarat, Durga welcomed in Bengal's pavilions like a daughter home for a few days, golu dolls on steps in the South. Four ways of keeping the same nights. But here's the custom that surprises people most. On the eighth or ninth day, many families invite young girls from the neighborhood into the house. They wash the girls' feet, mark their foreheads, seat them like honored guests and feed them, often puri, chickpeas and a sweet halwa, with a small gift at the end. It's called kanya puja, and the girls are honored as forms of the Goddess herself. The nine faces from yesterday, sitting on the floor of an ordinary living room. And on the tenth day, Vijayadashami, the victory. Ravana's effigy burns in the North. Durga goes back to the river in Bengal. And in some homes, the green shoots from the tray are shared out as a blessing. The seed went in on the first morning. On the tenth day, you hand out what grew.
screen: `GHATASTHAPANA: SETTING UP THE POT.` · `A FAST THAT KEEPS TIME.` · `KANYA PUJA: GIRLS AS THE GODDESS.` · `THE TENTH DAY: HAND OUT WHAT GREW.` · then, large: `WELCOMED, HONORED, VICTORIOUS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plant nine nights. You don't need a pot of barley. Settle, and breathe. Think of one small thing you'd like to see grow: a habit, a kindness, a steadiness. Now picture a tray of soil, and press that one thing in like a seed. You'll come back to it for nine nights. Tonight is the first. Just breathe beside it. You don't make a seed sprout by staring at it. You keep the nights, and it does the rest. The bell holds the time.
Navaratri. Nine nights of the Goddess, kept with a pot and seeds, a fast, girls honored as her forms, and the tenth day's victory.
Your line: Navaratri, nine nights, nine forms, Durga. Today, name the seed you planted, and give it one minute tonight. Then nine nights. Day one hundred forty-four.

145.title: Janmashtami (midnight; Krishna's birth)
145.hook: a whole house awake at a quarter to twelve, a tiny cradle, and a fast that breaks at midnight
145.tomorrow: Ganesh Chaturthi (the clay idol; the immersion)
145.howItsDone: On Janmashtami many Hindus fast until midnight, sing and retell Krishna's birth in homes and temples, and at midnight bathe an image of baby Krishna in panchamrita, dress him, and rock him in a cradle before breaking the fast; in Maharashtra, dahi handi follows the next day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Navaratri as it's kept: a pot, sprouting barley, circles of dancers, dolls on steps. How's the seed you planted? Today, one night, and the clock that matters is midnight. Day one hundred forty-five.

It's eleven forty-five at night, and nobody in the house is asleep. The kids were supposed to be in bed hours ago; they're wide awake. Grandma hasn't eaten since morning. There's a tiny wooden cradle in the corner, hung with flowers, and in it a little image of a baby. The temple down the road is packed, and people are singing the same few lines over and over, louder as the minutes pass. Someone is watching the clock. At midnight, the conch shells blow, the bells go wild, and everyone shouts. Nothing happened, and everything did. This is Janmashtami, and you already know the story. Today is how it's kept.
screen: `ELEVEN FORTY-FIVE. NOBODY'S ASLEEP.` → `A CRADLE WITH FLOWERS.` → `AT MIDNIGHT, THE CONCH.`

segments.voice: The story, from the Bhagavata Purana: Krishna born at midnight in Kamsa's prison, carried across the flooded Yamuna, hidden among cowherds. Janma, birth. Ashtami, the eighth day of the dark half of the month, usually in August or September. The festival turns that story into a night you live through. First, the fast. Many people eat nothing, or only fruit and milk, from morning until midnight. It isn't a punishment. It's waiting, with your body. Second, the night itself. Temples and homes stay awake, singing bhajans and retelling the story, sometimes acting it out, so that by midnight you've walked the whole road from the prison to the river. Third, the moment. At midnight the image of baby Krishna is bathed, the way you'd bathe a newborn, in milk, yogurt, honey, ghee and sugar mixed together, called panchamrita, the five nectars. He's dressed in new clothes, laid in the cradle, and the cradle is rocked. People take turns giving it a push. Then the food: often sweets made with butter, because the baby Krishna of the stories is a famous butter thief. And the fast breaks. The next day, in Maharashtra, comes dahi handi: a pot of curd hung high above the street, and young people climb on each other's shoulders in a human pyramid to break it, just like little Krishna and his friends raiding the butter pots. Notice what the whole night teaches. You can't make midnight come faster. You can only stay awake, and be ready when it does.
screen: `JANMA, BIRTH. ASHTAMI, THE EIGHTH.` · `A FAST: WAITING WITH YOUR BODY.` · `THE BATH, THE CRADLE, THE PUSH.` · `A POT OF CURD, A HUMAN PYRAMID.` · then, large: `STAY AWAKE, AND BE READY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rock the cradle. Settle, and breathe. Picture that tiny cradle hung with flowers, in a room full of people who've been waiting all day. Now it's your turn. Reach out and give it one small push. Watch it swing away, and come back. Breathe out as it swings away. Breathe in as it comes back. Keep it gentle. There's a newborn in there. If you pray, you can say Krishna's name once with each swing. If not, just keep the rhythm, and wait with everyone else. The bell holds the time.
Janmashtami. Krishna's birth, on the eighth day of the dark half of the month, kept with a fast, a vigil, and a cradle rocked at midnight.
Your line: Janmashtami, midnight, Krishna's birth. Today, wait well for one thing. Don't refresh it, don't rush it. Stay ready. Day one hundred forty-five.

146.title: Ganesh Chaturthi (the clay idol; the immersion)
146.hook: a clay Ganesha carried home under a cloth, drums in the street, and a moon nobody is supposed to look at
146.carry: Ganesh Chaturthi (the clay idol; the immersion)
146.tomorrow: Ganesh Chaturthi (the clay idol; the immersion)
146.howItsDone: On Ganesh Chaturthi many Hindus bring a clay image of Ganesha home or to a neighborhood pavilion, invite his presence with prana pratishtha, and honor him daily with flowers, durva grass, modak and arti for one and a half to ten days.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Janmashtami: a fast, a cradle, and midnight. What did you wait for, and did you wait well? Today, a god who arrives at your front door, made of clay. Day one hundred forty-six.

In Maharashtra, in late summer, you'll see a family walking home from the market carrying a Ganesha about the size of a toddler. His face is covered with a cloth. A cousin is banging a drum. The kids are shouting Ganpati Bappa Morya. He's made of clay, still slightly damp. At home, a corner has been cleared, a little platform set up, flowers ready. They'll uncover his face only once he's in his seat. For the next few days he's a guest, fed, sung to, visited. Then they'll carry him back out and give him to the water. Today, the arrival.
screen: `A CLAY GANESHA, FACE COVERED.` → `GANPATI BAPPA MORYA.` → `A GUEST FOR A FEW DAYS.`

segments.voice: Chaturthi means the fourth day, the fourth of the bright half of the month of Bhadrapada, in August or September, and that's the day Ganesha is said to have been born. And why clay? Go back to the very first story on this path. Parvati makes a son from earth, from the paste of her own bath, and sets him to guard her door. Ganesha begins as something shaped by hand. So the clay makes sense: once a year, families shape him again, or bring home one that's been shaped. At home the image is set on its seat, and a priest or an elder performs prana pratishtha, inviting life into it. From that moment he's treated as present. He gets fresh flowers, blades of durva grass, which he's said to love, and modak, the sweet dumplings he's always holding. Arti morning and evening. Here's a surprise from history. For a long time this was mostly a festival inside homes. Then in 1893, in Pune, the freedom fighter Bal Gangadhar Tilak helped turn it into a great public festival, with Ganeshas in the street, where whole neighborhoods could gather, under British rule, with a god everyone loved. Today some public Ganeshas are two stories tall. And one odd custom. On this night, many people won't look at the moon. The story people tell: the moon laughed at Ganesha, round and full of sweets, after a tumble, and Ganesha cursed him, so anyone who looks at the moon that night will be falsely accused. It's a funny story with a sharp point: mocking someone costs you more than it costs them.

147.title: Ganesh Chaturthi (the clay idol; the immersion)
147.hook: after days as a guest, Ganesha is carried to the water, and the crowd asks him to come back sooner next year
147.carry: Ganesh Chaturthi (the clay idol; the immersion)
147.howItsDone: At the end of Ganesh Chaturthi, after one and a half to ten days, many Hindus perform a final arti and carry the clay Ganesha in procession to a river, lake or the sea for visarjan, chanting Ganpati Bappa Morya; many now use plain clay or immerse at home.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ganesh Chaturthi: the clay Ganesha carried home, invited in, and treated as a guest. Did you clear a space? Today, the hard part: letting him go. And a look back at the week. Day one hundred forty-seven.

It's the last day. The Ganesha who's been sitting in the living room, fed and sung to, is lifted off his seat. The family does one last arti. Then out the door, into a street that's become a river of people: drums, dancing, colored powder, a thousand Ganeshas moving slowly toward the sea. At the shore, people wade in up to their waists and lower him into the water. He slips under. And the whole beach shouts the same thing: Ganpati Bappa Morya, pudhchya varshi lavkar ya. Father Ganesha, come early next year. A lot of people are crying.
screen: `ONE LAST ARTI.` → `A RIVER OF PEOPLE TO THE SEA.` → `COME EARLY NEXT YEAR.`

segments.voice: The immersion is called visarjan, from a Sanskrit root that means to let go, to release. It happens on different days in different homes: after a day and a half, or three, five, seven, and the biggest crowds on the tenth day, called Anant Chaturdashi. So why make a god from clay, give him a room, feed him for days, and then drown him? Here's how many Hindus explain it. The clay image was never the whole of Ganesha. He was invited into it, and now he's sent off, back to wherever he's always been. The clay goes back to the water and the earth it came from. What was shaped by hand is unshaped again. Nothing is kept. And that's the practice hiding in the festival: welcome something fully, and then let it go fully. Don't keep the image on a shelf out of fear of losing it. The goodbye is part of the love. There's an honest problem in the modern festival too. Many big images are made of plaster and painted with chemical colors, and they don't dissolve; they pile up in rivers and the sea. So many families have gone back to plain clay, sometimes immersing their Ganesha in a bucket at home and pouring the water on the garden. The old form turns out to be the kinder one. And this week, look what you've walked through. Holi's fire and colors. Navaratri's nine faces and nine nights. Janmashtami's midnight cradle. Ganesha arriving, and leaving. Four festivals. Each one a way of living a story with your hands.
screen: `VISARJAN: TO LET GO.` · `THE CLAY GOES BACK TO THE WATER.` · `WELCOME FULLY, RELEASE FULLY.` · `THE WEEK: FIRE, NIGHTS, CRADLE, CLAY.` · then, large: `THE GOODBYE IS PART OF THE LOVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: carry him to the water. Settle, and breathe. Picture the Ganesha you welcomed yesterday, sitting in the space you cleared. Now think of one thing in your life that's had its season: a plan that's done, a role you've outgrown, a worry you've been hosting. Set it in his lap. Lift him up. Walk slowly, with the drums, to the water's edge. Wade in. Lower him gently, and let go. Watch the water close. If you like, say it with the crowd, silently: come again next year. The bell holds the time.
Ganesh Chaturthi. He arrives in clay on the fourth day, stays as a guest, and is given back to the water, with a promise to come again.
Your line: Ganesh Chaturthi, the clay idol, the immersion. Today, finish one goodbye properly: return the borrowed thing, close the old tab, say thank you for a season. Day one hundred forty-seven.
